paragraphs.text: This cake's leaf comes from [Yiwu](greater-yiwu:where-it-is), in the north of Mengla County in Xishuangbanna, east of the Lancang River. It is one of the old Six Famous Tea Mountains, and its town has long been where tea from the surrounding villages is gathered and processed.

The cake dates from the 1980s. At about forty-one years, it sits well inside what the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, so how it was kept matters as much as how long.

The leaf was made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition). It was heaped warm and damp so that it could be drunk soon after making instead of after years of waiting, then pressed into a cake. Yunnan's factories first brought [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) into production in 1973, so this tea comes from the method's first two decades.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
